Calculus is the mathematics of change and accumulation. Derivatives measure how fast something changes; integrals add up small pieces into a whole; and the fundamental theorem of calculus says these two operations undo each other. Almost everything else in a calculus course, from optimization to series to differential equations, is built from those ideas.

This article collects 100 formulas and theorems that a student meets across single-variable calculus, series, multivariable calculus, vector calculus and a first look at differential equations. For each one you get the statement, the conditions under which it holds (theorems are only as good as their hypotheses), and a short worked example. Every example was recomputed with SymPy before publication.

The basic differentiation and integration rules also appear, more briefly, in 100 mathematics formulas every student should know. This article goes further: it states the theorems behind the rules and covers series, several variables and vector fields. All angles are in radians.

Common mistakes

  • Using a theorem without its hypotheses. The mean value theorem needs continuity on the closed interval and differentiability inside; L'Hôpital's rule only applies to 0/00/00/0 or ∞/∞\infty/\infty∞/∞ forms.
  • Dropping the inner derivative in the chain rule. ddxsin⁡(x2)=2xcos⁡(x2)\frac{d}{dx}\sin(x^2) = 2x\cos(x^2)dxd​sin(x2)=2xcos(x2), not cos⁡(x2)\cos(x^2)cos(x2).
  • Forgetting to change the limits in a substitution. Either change them to uuu-values or substitute back before evaluating.
  • Assuming an→0a_n \to 0an​→0 means the series converges. The harmonic series is the standard counterexample (formula 62).
  • Forgetting the Jacobian. In polar coordinates dA=r dr dθdA = r\,dr\,d\thetadA=rdrdθ, not dr dθdr\,d\thetadrdθ.

  • Using degrees. Every derivative and series of a trigonometric function in this article assumes radians.
